scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do yet always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I do not pay rent either, which is why I have been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone and uni fees). He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being AITA (A**hole I**n**ternet **T**hink **A**bout) for refusing to lend my brother my vacation money. Let me start by understanding the situation. My brother and I live with our parents. He's 30 and went back to school after a bad job, which is why he moved back in about 11 months ago. I'm 21, in my third year of university, working to put myself through business school, which I find difficult but manageable. I plan to graduate in two years. When I started university, I began saving a bit from each paycheck, sometimes as much as 15%, other times as low as 1%, to go on a big vacation after graduation. I'm thinking of a cruise, Japan, or a trip to different European countries. My savings are around $2800 now. My brother hasn't been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. Our parents already help him financially, so he wouldn't ask them for more help for that. Last week, when he was complaining to my parents about needing a vacation, they mentioned me and my vacation fund, suggesting he could have been doing something similar all these years to afford a trip or start now to maybe go across country in a year. Three days ago, he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or fall. He said since I won't need it for another two years, there's plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do, but he always seems broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I don't pay rent either, which is why I've been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as all my makeup, health supplies, phone, and uni fees). He's very mad that I said no. He says it's not fair because, as the youngest child, I get to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it's not fair that I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went, whereas he had to go back. He says I've only been able to save so much money because mom and dad spoiled me. I disagree. My father, as well as my university accounting and finance classes, taught me to budget. If anything, I think my parents spoiled him because he doesn't know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don't think it's fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he'll be able to pay me back in time. Even if he could, I'm uncomfortable with the idea. So, is it AITA for me to refuse to lend him my vacation money? Let me think through this step by step. First, I need to understand what AITA means. From what I know, AITA is a term used to describe someone who is being overly harsh or unreasonable in a situation, often involving money or personal boundaries. It's about whether the person's actions are justified or if they're being too strict or unfair. In this case, I'm refusing to lend my brother money that I've been saving for my future vacation. He's in a tough spot financially, trying to go back to school and manage his money, but he's also been living with our parents and receiving financial help from them. He's asking to borrow money that I've set aside for my own goals, and I'm concerned about his ability to pay it back, as well as the fairness of the situation. I need to consider several factors: 1. **Financial Responsibility**: Am I being responsible by not lending him money? He has a history of being bad with money, and I'm worried he won't be able to pay me back. Is it fair for me to prioritize my own financial goals over his needs? 2. **Family Dynamics**: There seems to be some tension regarding how our parents have treated us differently. He feels that I've been spoiled more, which is affecting his perspective. How does this family history influence the current situation? 3. **Personal Boundaries**: Is it reasonable for me to set boundaries regarding my savings? Do I have the right to protect my own financial future, even if it means disappointing my brother? 4. **Alternative Solutions**: Are there other ways to help him without jeopardizing my own plans? Could we find a middle ground where he can save his own money for a trip, or perhaps we can discuss a smaller loan with a clear repayment plan? 5. **Emotional Impact**: How does this refusal affect our relationship? Is the potential strain worth the protection of my savings, or should I consider his emotional well-being in my decision? 6. **Long-term Consequences**: What are the long-term implications of lending him money? Could this set a precedent for future financial requests, and how would that affect our relationship? Considering these points, I need to weigh the pros and cons of my decision. On one hand, I'm protecting my own financial security and ensuring that I can achieve my goals after graduation. On the other hand, I'm refusing to help my brother, who is in a difficult situation and feels that he's been treated unfairly by our parents. I also need to think about whether there's a way to compromise. Maybe I could lend him a smaller amount, or perhaps we could discuss a repayment plan that works for both of us. Alternatively, I could suggest that he start saving now, even if it's a small amount each month, so he can afford his own trip in the future. Another angle is to consider the role of our parents in this situation. They mentioned my vacation fund as a way for him to save, but they also help him financially. Is it fair for them to suggest that he use my savings when they are already providing support? It seems like they might be trying to shift the responsibility onto me, which could be contributing to the tension. I also need to reflect on the fairness aspect. My brother feels that I've been favored more in terms of financial support from our parents, which is making him resentful. I disagree with his assessment, but I can see how his perspective is shaped by his experiences. Understanding his feelings, even if I don't agree with them, is important in navigating this situation. In terms of personal boundaries, it's crucial for me to protect my own financial well-being. I've worked hard to save this money, and it's for a goal that I've been looking forward to for years. Lending it to my brother, especially without a solid repayment plan, could put my own plans at risk. It's important to respect my own needs and priorities, even if it means disappointing someone else. However, I also don't want our relationship to suffer because of this. Communication is key. Maybe I can sit down with my brother and have an open conversation about our financial situations, our goals, and how we can support each other without compromising our individual plans. This might help us find a middle ground and improve our relationship rather than creating more tension. In summary, while I understand my brother's need for a vacation and his frustration with the situation, I also have valid reasons for refusing to lend him my vacation money. My financial security and personal goals are important, and I need to protect them. However, communication and finding alternative solutions could help mitigate the conflict and maintain our relationship.
